The slider’s minimum and maximum are a workspace setting. Adjust scale saves as soon as you click Apply, even if you don’t save the lead, and changes the slider on every lead for everyone in the workspace.
Qualified leads become projects and move to the Converted tab. See Turning a lead into a project.
If your workspace is on Solo, you can still open and view existing leads. You can’t create, edit, move or delete them.
Only owners and admins can delete leads, and deleting one is permanent. Nothing blocks the delete, because a lead has no invoices attached.
Confirm in the Delete Lead dialog.
Converted leads can’t be deleted from the leads page. They are projects now.
How to convert a qualified lead into a project, the two kinds of project you can create, what carries over, and what blocks converting.

/help/invoice-statuses.title: Invoices and their statuses ⋅ Billow
/help/invoice-statuses.description: What each invoice status means, how an invoice moves between them, how to find, rename, duplicate, delete and restore invoices, and how numbering works.
h2: Currency and tax on project invoices
When an invoice cannot be restored
h3: What your client sees when you send an invoice
p: What each invoice status means, how an invoice moves between them, how to find, rename, duplicate, delete and restore invoices, and how numbering works.
Every invoice in Billow has one of four statuses. The status decides what you can still change, and it moves in one direction only: Draft → Pending → Paid → Refunded.
You are still working on it. It has no number, and nobody outside your workspace can see it. You can edit everything.
You sent it or shared its link. It has a number and can no longer be edited.
Awaiting Payment, Due upon receipt, or the number of days overdue, such as 3d Overdue
Your client paid, or you marked it paid.
The payment went back to your client. This is a final status.
Imported invoices carry an extra Imported badge next to their status.
You send the invoice or copy its public link
Your client pays by card, or you mark it paid. See Getting paid
You refund the invoice, or your client wins a card dispute
No other change is possible. A sent invoice cannot go back to Draft, and a paid invoice cannot go back to Pending.
You cannot edit it or put it back to draft.
Copying the public link counts as sending. It assigns the number and locks the invoice in the same way, and Billow warns you before it happens.
Check the figures while the invoice is still a draft. To fix a sent invoice, replace it with a corrected copy.
Go to Invoices to see all your invoices. Three tabs sit above the list. The Refunded tab only appears once you have a refunded invoice.
Pending invoices, overdue and soonest due first, with your drafts in a Drafts section below them
Paid invoices, most recently paid first
Refunded invoices, most recently refunded first
Each row in the Drafts section has a Send Invoice button that opens the send dialog. If the draft cannot be sent yet, the button is disabled and shows the reason when you hover over it.

The columns are Invoice, Account, Project, Type, Amount, Due and Status. Due shows the date the invoice is due. On the Paid tab, a Paid column with the payment date replaces it, and on the Refunded tab a Refunded column with the refund date.

You can sort by any column and filter by Account, Project, Contact, Type, Source, Currency, Amount, Invoice date and Due date. The Paid tab adds a Paid date filter, and the Unpaid tab adds a Stage filter for Overdue or Awaiting payment invoices. See Filtering and sorting lists.
Each row has a … menu at its right end.
Invoices created in Billow, and invoices imported from a CSV
Invoices imported from a PDF or image. It returns the original file
Every invoice, for owners and admins only, unless a deletion rule blocks it
Renaming changes the title only. You can rename drafts and imported invoices.
Open the … menu on the invoice’s row.
Enter the new title under Name.
On an imported invoice, Rename is also in the … menu on the invoice page. Everything else on an imported invoice stays as it was imported. On a draft, you can change the title with Edit instead.
Duplicating creates a new draft with the same account, project, contact, line items, payment method, currency, tax and note.
Open the … menu at the top right of the page.
The new draft opens straight away. It is dated today, keeps the same payment term, and adds “(copy)” to the title if the original had one.
You cannot duplicate a deposit invoice, or an invoice on a completed, cancelled or rejected project. For a completed project, reopen the project first.
A sent invoice cannot be edited. To correct one, follow Correct a sent invoice.

When you create an invoice, the Due field offers Immediately, 15 days or 30 days from the invoice date. 30 days is the default, and it is also what automatically drafted invoices get. Immediately means the invoice is due on receipt.
Billow numbers an invoice when you send it, in the format INV-YYYY-NNNN, for example INV-2026-0001. Numbers count up within each year and start again from 0001 in January.
A draft has no number, so drafts never leave gaps.
Deleting a sent invoice does not free its number.
Imported invoices keep the number from your old tool and do not affect Billow’s numbering.
A regular invoice has line items you write yourself.

A deposit invoice belongs to an accepted offer and bills a percentage of it. A project can have one deposit invoice. Billow drafts it for you when your client accepts the offer. You can also create one by hand while the project has no deposit invoice yet: the invoice form then shows an Invoice Type choice, set to Regular Invoice by default.
The type is set when you create the invoice and cannot be changed afterwards. See Deposits and automatic invoices.
On a project with an offer, the invoice takes its currency and tax from the offer. See Invoices on a project.
Only owners and admins can delete invoices. A deleted invoice moves to the deleted invoices page, where an owner or admin can restore it.
Open the invoice, or find it in the invoice list.
Delete Invoice Are you sure you want to delete [invoice]? This invoice will move to deleted invoices. Its number stays reserved and you can restore it later.
Two rules can block a deletion. Delete Invoice is then disabled, with the reason on it.
No. “Cannot delete an invoice paid through Stripe.”
A deposit invoice while the project still has regular invoices
Not yet. “Cannot delete deposit invoice while regular invoices exist for this project.” Delete the regular invoices first
Marked paid by hand, or paid by bank transfer
A deleted invoice keeps its Billow number, whether it was paid or not. Deleting an imported invoice frees the number from your old tool, so you can import a corrected version.
Only owners and admins can restore invoices.
Click Deleted invoices at the bottom of the list. The link only appears when you have deleted invoices.
Click the restore button at the end of the invoice’s row.
The invoice comes back with its original number, status and paid date, and its figures are unchanged. If its project was deleted in the meantime, the dialog tells you:
The project this invoice belonged to was deleted. The invoice will be restored without a project.
The invoice then comes back as a standalone invoice.
Four situations block a restore. The restore button is then disabled, with the reason on it.
It is an imported invoice and its number now belongs to another invoice
“Cannot restore: invoice number 2024-017 is now used by another invoice.”
“Cannot restore: the client has been deleted.”
It is a deposit invoice and its project was deleted
“Cannot restore: the project has been deleted.” A deposit invoice must belong to a project
It is a deposit invoice and the project already has another one
“Cannot restore: the project already has a deposit invoice.”
What is on the invoice page your client opens, how they pay by card or bank transfer, and how long the link keeps working.

/help/importing-invoices.title: Importing past invoices ⋅ Billow
/help/importing-invoices.description: How to import invoices from another tool, which files you can upload, how to review and fix rows before importing, and what the imported invoices look like.
h3: What your client sees when you send an invoice
p: How to import invoices from another tool, which files you can upload, how to review and fix rows before importing, and what the imported invoices look like.

You can upload the invoices you issued in another tool. Billow reads them, creates the invoices together with the accounts and contacts they name, and adds them to your revenue history. Only the workspace owner can import.
Imports are for your history, and importing doesn’t email your clients. To get Billow numbering, public links and payment tracking, create new invoices in Billow.
A connected AI assistant creates new Billow invoices and cannot import past ones.
Drag your files into the upload area, or click it to browse.
Check the list of files. Remove any you don’t want with the trash button next to it.
Click the Import button. It shows how many files you added, for example Import 3 files.
Billow confirms with “Import started.” and opens the import while it analyzes the files in the background. You can leave the page. Billow emails you when the import is ready to review.
Reads each invoice with AI and picks out the number, dates, account, line items and totals
Treats each row as one invoice and works out which column holds what
Each import takes up to 100 files. Each file can be up to 2 MB, and a PDF can have up to 10 pages.
A file you have already imported cannot be uploaded again. It stays blocked while its import is still open, or once it has become an invoice in Billow.
A CSV needs one row per invoice. If your old tool exports one row per line item, combine the rows first or upload the PDFs instead.
If Billow cannot use a CSV, the review screen lists it under Rejected files with the reason:
Several rows for the same invoice
“This CSV has multiple rows per invoice (line-item export). Consolidate to one row per invoice, or upload PDFs instead.”
“This CSV does not look like invoice data.”
“This CSV is missing required columns for: …” followed by the missing fields
A header row but no invoices
“This CSV has a header but no data rows.”
Billow creates nothing until you confirm the import.
Open the link in the email, or go to Settings → Imports and click Review now next to the import.
Check the invoices under Will be imported and Won’t be imported. Hover over a row’s status to see why it needs attention.
To fix a row, click its edit button, correct the details in the Edit invoice panel, and click Save changes.
To leave a row out, click its trash button. You can bring it back with the restore button.
Check the Accounts and Contacts lists. Each entry is marked Matched if it already exists in Billow, or New if the import creates it.
Click Import into Billow. The button shows how many invoices are ready, for example Import into Billow (12).
Check the counts in the Confirm import dialog and click the Import button, for example Import 12 invoices.
The Confirm import dialog lists how many invoices, new accounts and new contacts the import creates. If some rows still need review, it also warns you:
[number] invoices still marked “Needs review” will be discarded, including their uploaded files. This can’t be undone.
Only rows marked Ready are imported. To include a row that needs review, fix it before you confirm.
Billow thinks the file is not an invoice, or you removed the row

If Billow decides a file is not an invoice, the row says so: “Our system thinks this is not an invoice. If it’s mistaken, you can fill in the details by clicking the edit button.” Saving the row in the Edit invoice panel overrides that decision and checks the row again.
“Missing: …” followed by the missing fields, for example “Missing: Date, Total.”
“Pick or create an account for this invoice.”
Choose an existing account or create a new one
“Confirm the matched account for this invoice.”
Check that Billow picked the right account
“This invoice number already exists in this workspace.”
Check whether the invoice is already in Billow
“Another row in this import has the same invoice number.”
Remove the duplicate or correct the number
“The amounts on this invoice do not add up.”
“We could not read this invoice currency.”
“This invoice is dated in the future.”
“We had to guess this file’s date format. Check the date and save to confirm.”
Check the date and save the row
Fill in the details by hand
“The invoice number is too long (max 64 characters).”
They are marked Paid, with an extra Imported badge. The paid date is the one on the invoice, or its invoice date if it has none.
They keep the number from your old tool, exactly as it was. Billow’s own INV- numbering is not affected.
They are not attached to a project, so the import creates no projects or offers.
For PDF and image imports, Billow stores the original file with the invoice. Download imported invoice in the invoice’s … menu returns it, and it is included in your data export.
You can rename them from the … menu in the invoice list or on the invoice page. Every other field stays as imported.
Settings → Imports lists your past imports with their status.
Billow is still reading the files
The review screen is ready for you
The import was not finished within 7 days, so Billow removed its files
Something went wrong while processing. Upload the files again
Finish reviewing within 7 days, or Billow removes the files. Billow emails you if an import fails.
Click Cancel next to the import.
Click Cancel import in the dialog.
Billow deletes the uploaded files. This cannot be undone.
An admin can delete an imported invoice like any other invoice, including one that is Paid. Deleting it frees its number and its file, so you can import a corrected version.
What is on the invoice page your client opens, how they pay by card or bank transfer, and how long the link keeps working.

/help/how-billow-works.title: How Billow works ⋅ Billow
/help/how-billow-works.description: The building blocks of Billow, how work moves from lead to payment, the two kinds of project, how to use search, and where to start.
p: The building blocks of Billow, how work moves from lead to payment, the two kinds of project, how to use search, and where to start.
Billow is built around the project. A project is one piece of work for one account, and it holds the invoices you bill for that work and the offer, if you send one.
One piece of work for one account
The proposal you send your client for a project
A bill, usually for a project
Your workspace holds the settings that new documents start from: currency, tax rate, default deposit, bank details and contract terms. See Setting up your workspace.
Work in Billow follows this path:
You track an opportunity as a lead on the pipeline board.
You create a project, either directly or by converting the lead.
You build an offer on the project and send it to your client.
Your client accepts the offer, signing the contract if it includes one, and the project becomes Active.
Billow drafts the invoices from the offer, and you send them.
A project can skip the lead, the offer, or both.
In the “What kind of project?” dialog, choose Project with offer or Simple project.
Billow opens the offer wizard for a project with an offer, or a short form for a simple project.
The full path. You build an offer with deliverables and prices, finish the setup, and send it from the project page when you’re ready.
A link to the offer, where they accept or reject it
A place for invoices for work that doesn’t need a proposal, such as a retainer or an hourly month
Nothing until you send an invoice
If your client accepts an offer, the project becomes Active and Billow drafts your invoices.
You can add an offer to a simple project later with Turn into offer, as long as the project is Active and has no invoices. Once an offer is attached, it can’t be removed. See Simple projects.

A lead is an opportunity you haven’t committed to yet. It stays on the pipeline board until you click Convert to Project. Converting creates the project, carries the account and the contact over, and takes the lead off the board. See Turning a lead into a project.
The lead pipeline is available on the Grow and Scale plans. On any plan, you can create projects directly without a lead.

When your client accepts an offer, Billow creates the invoices for the whole engagement as drafts. The deposit percentage on the offer decides how many invoices there are and how much each one is for:
At 50%, you get a deposit invoice and a final invoice.
At 0%, you get a single invoice for the full amount.
Billow sends none of them. The drafts wait in your invoice list until you choose a payment method and send each one yourself.
You set the deposit on the offer before you send it, and it decides the whole billing schedule. Deposits and automatic invoices covers every option.
Search finds your accounts, contacts, projects, leads and invoices. Results appear once you type three characters.
To open search, do one of these:
Press ⌘K on a Mac, or Ctrl+K on Windows.
Press / while you’re not typing in a field.
The same box also does the following:
Creates things, with Add new lead, Start new project, Create new invoice, Add new contact and Add new account. Add new lead needs the Grow or Scale plan.
Opens your user and workspace settings.
Add an account and a contact.
Invoice it, or build an offer and send it.
How to sign up, verify your email, create your workspace and pick a plan, then complete the setup checklist on your Cockpit.

/help/getting-paid.title: Getting paid ⋅ Billow
/help/getting-paid.description: How to choose between bank transfer and card, mark an invoice as paid, resend it and send a reminder, and what your client receives after paying.
h3: What your client sees when you send an invoice
p: How to choose between bank transfer and card, mark an invoice as paid, resend it and send a reminder, and what your client receives after paying.
Every invoice has one payment method, either bank transfer or card. You choose it on the draft, and it decides how your client pays and how the invoice becomes Paid.
From their own bank, using the account details on the invoice
Automatically, once Stripe confirms the payment
A bank account in Settings → Accounting
Open the … menu at the top right of the page and choose Edit.
Under Payment Method, choose Card Payment (Stripe) or Bank Transfer.
If you chose Bank Transfer, pick the account under Bank Account. Add new opens a form to add another account.

You can also set the payment method on the Create Invoice form when you create the invoice. Until an invoice has one, its page shows a warning with an Add Payment Method button, and you cannot send it. See When sending is blocked.

If you choose Bank Transfer before adding any bank account, the form shows “You first need to add a bank account to use Bank Transfer” with a Set up now button. If you choose Card Payment (Stripe) without an active Stripe connection, it shows “You first need to connect Stripe to Billow to use Card Payments”. In both cases, saving is refused until the method is set up.

Your account details appear on the invoice, with a copy button next to each field, so your client can paste them into their banking app. Billow is not notified when the money arrives, so you mark the invoice as paid yourself.
Open the … menu at the top right of the page.
In the Mark Invoice as Paid dialog, pick the date the payment arrived. It defaults to today.
The invoice changes to Paid, and the date you picked becomes its paid date. Future dates cannot be picked. Any team member can mark an invoice as paid.
Mark as paid is only available on sent invoices. On a draft it is disabled with “Draft invoices must be sent first”.

Your client pays on Stripe’s checkout page. When Stripe confirms the payment, the invoice changes to Paid without any action from you. See What your client sees when you send an invoice for the payment flow on their side.
Enter your client’s email address under Send via email. If the invoice has a contact, the hint below the field shows their address, and clicking it fills it in.
Billow emails the same link again. You can resend as often as you need.

You can send a reminder once an invoice is overdue, or straight away if it’s due upon receipt. Billow never sends reminders on its own. The Reminder button sits on the invoice’s status badge, which reads “Due upon receipt” or shows the days overdue.

The reminder goes to the email address of the invoice’s contact. If the contact has no email address, Send Email stays disabled and the invoice list shows no Reminder button, so add one to the contact first.
Open the invoice, or find it in the invoice list.
Click Reminder on its status badge.
Click the subject to change it.

The default subject is “Open Invoice”, and the default message reminds your client that the invoice was due and links to it. To add invoice details, type { in the subject or message and pick a variable. Billow fills it in when the email is sent.
Billow emails the team member who created an invoice when:
Invoice emails, including reminders, go out under your workspace’s legal name. The default reminder message is signed with your first name.
Billow does not send your client a payment confirmation. For card payments, Stripe may send its own receipt. For bank transfers, your client receives nothing.
To reverse a payment, see Refunding an invoice.
What is on the invoice page your client opens, how they pay by card or bank transfer, and how long the link keeps working.

/help/deposits-and-auto-invoices.title: Deposits and automatic invoices ⋅ Billow
/help/deposits-and-auto-invoices.description: What Billow drafts when your client accepts an offer, how the deposit percentage sets the schedule, how to send the drafts, and how to create a deposit invoice yourself.
h3: What your client sees when you send an invoice
p: What Billow drafts when your client accepts an offer, how the deposit percentage sets the schedule, how to send the drafts, and how to create a deposit invoice yourself.

When your client accepts an offer, Billow drafts every invoice for the project. The deposit percentage on the offer decides how many invoices you get and what each one bills. Nothing is sent automatically.
The invoices appear a few seconds after your client accepts the offer. They show up as drafts in the Drafts section of the Unpaid tab in your invoice list, and on the project.
You set the percentage under Upfront Deposit when you build the offer. There are five options.
One invoice for the full amount
The number of invoices follows from the percentage. You cannot set it separately. For a different split, delete the drafts you don’t need and create your own invoices on the project.
With no deposit, the single invoice has no title and shows as Invoice. Titled invoices only appear when there is a deposit.
The same project with a 25% deposit:
The same project with a 33% deposit:
The deposit takes exactly 33%. The rest is split evenly between the other two invoices, so each of them is larger than the deposit.
Any leftover cents go on the last invoice. The invoices always add up to exactly the accepted total.
Today’s date as the issue date, due in 30 days
The project’s account and main contact
The offer’s currency and tax settings, which stay locked
The offer’s Hide deliverable prices setting, which you can change on each draft

If the project has a deposit invoice, send that one first. The other invoices on the project cannot be sent until the deposit invoice is paid. Until then, Send Invoice is disabled with “The deposit invoice for this project must be paid first.”
Until you send them, you can change amounts, dates and line items on regular drafts, or delete the ones you don’t need.
Go to Invoices and open the draft from the Drafts section.
Open the … menu at the top right of the page and choose Edit.
Under Payment Method, choose Card Payment (Stripe) or Bank Transfer.
Change anything else you need, such as the dates or line items.
Click Send Invoice and follow the dialog.
The invoice changes to Pending and your client receives the link. How each payment method works is covered in Getting paid.
A deposit invoice lists the full project scope, with every deliverable at its real price, and bills only the deposit amount. Your client sees it with a badge such as “50% Deposit”.
A deposit invoice is more locked than a regular invoice, including while it is a draft:
The line items come from the offer and cannot be edited.
The account and project cannot be changed.
The currency and tax fields show “Locked for deposit invoices”.
The amount follows the offer’s deposit percentage.
You can still set the payment method, the dates and whether your client sees the deliverable prices.
Deposit invoices cannot be duplicated. A deposit invoice cannot be deleted while the project has regular invoices.
Go to Invoices and click Create Invoice.
Choose the account, then the project.
Under Invoice Type, choose Deposit Invoice.
Choose a payment method and set the dates.
The line items fill in from the offer and bill the deposit amount.
The Invoice Type field only appears when all of these are true:
The project’s offer has a deposit.
The project has no deposit invoice, other than a refunded one.
Otherwise every new invoice is a regular invoice, and there is nothing to choose. Refunding the existing deposit invoice makes the choice available again.
Invoice Type defaults to Regular Invoice. The type is set when you create the invoice and cannot be changed afterward, in either direction.
Upsells your client declined on the offer do not count toward the total and never appear on an invoice.
What is on the invoice page your client opens, how they pay by card or bank transfer, and how long the link keeps working.

/help/exporting-your-data.title: Exporting your data ⋅ Billow
/help/exporting-your-data.description: How to request and download a zip of your workspace data, what it contains, and how long it stays available.
h2: How long an export stays available
p: How to request and download a zip of your workspace data, what it contains, and how long it stays available.
Settings → Export produces one zip with everything in your workspace: your records as CSV spreadsheets and your documents as PDFs. Only owners see the Export tab and can request an export.
Wait for the email from Billow saying your export is ready.
Go back to Settings → Export and click Download.

After you click Request export, Billow confirms with “Export started. We will email you when it is ready.” The page shows “Preparing your export…” while Billow builds the zip. This usually takes a few minutes, and you can leave the page in the meantime.
Spreadsheets, one CSV per record type, which you can join by their ID columns:
PDFs of every invoice you’ve sent
PDFs of every offer that reached a client, plus its contract when the offer includes one
The original files of any invoices you imported from PDFs or images
For an invoice imported from a PDF or image, the zip holds the file exactly as you uploaded it.
Drafts appear in the CSVs but get no PDF.
An offer whose project ended up rejected or cancelled gets no PDF either.
Invoices imported from a CSV file appear in the CSVs but get no document.
Once your export is ready, Settings → Export shows “Available until [date].” Billow deletes the zip 7 days after it’s ready. Request a new one whenever you need it.
The download only works while you’re signed in as an owner of the workspace, so you can’t forward the link to someone else.
A workspace has one export at a time. While one is being prepared, you can’t request another, and Billow shows “An export is already being prepared.”

Once an export is ready, the page offers Request a new export next to Download. When the new export finishes, it replaces the previous one. While the new export is being prepared, the page no longer shows the previous one’s Download button, so download it first if you still need it.
If something goes wrong, Settings → Export shows “Something went wrong preparing your last export. Request a new one to try again.” Click Request export to start again.
Export stays available in read-only mode, so a lapsed subscription doesn’t stop you from taking your data with you.
Request an export before you cancel your subscription or delete your workspace.
How to set your default currency, tax rate, deposit percentage and business targets, and what each default changes.

/help/convert-lead-to-project.title: Turning a lead into a project ⋅ Billow
/help/convert-lead-to-project.description: How to convert a qualified lead into a project, the two kinds of project you can create, what carries over, and what blocks converting.
h1: Turning a lead into a project
h3: Filling in a lead from your notes
p: Turning a lead into a project
How to convert a qualified lead into a project, the two kinds of project you can create, what carries over, and what blocks converting.
Converting a lead turns it into a project. The project name, the account and the person of contact carry over. You can convert a lead once it is Qualified.
Qualifying and converting are two separate steps. Moving a lead to Qualified marks it as a good fit, and nothing else changes. The lead stays on the board until you convert it.
Only Qualified leads show the Convert to Project button. To qualify a lead, drag its card to the Qualified column, or open it and set the Stage to Qualified. See Tracking leads in your pipeline.
Go to Leads and find the Qualified lead.
Click Convert to Project on its card on the board, or on its row in the list.
In the What kind of project? dialog, choose Project with offer or Simple project.
Check the project details. Billow fills in the name, the account and the person of contact from the lead.
For a project with offer, click Save as Draft or Next: Deliverables. For a simple project, click Create Project.
The lead moves to the Converted tab. Its row there shows the project’s status and a View project button.
A project in Draft with an empty offer attached. The offer carries your workspace’s default deposit percentage and tax settings.
An Active project with no offer, ready to invoice
You can add an offer to a simple project later. See Building and sending an offer and Simple projects.
The lead’s details and notes stay with it. To see them, open the lead from the Converted tab. The page shows:
This lead was converted to a project and is now read-only.
Everything you change from then on happens on the project.
You’re at your plan’s active project limit
Complete a project, or move to a bigger plan. See Plans and limits.
At the limit, the project form shows:
You’ve reached your plan’s limit of [number] active projects. Complete a project or upgrade your plan to convert this lead.
Projects in Draft, Offer Pending and Active count toward the limit, so both kinds of project take a slot.
How to fill in a lead form from your notes, which fields autofill sets, how it matches accounts and contacts, and where your notes are processed.

/help/contracts-and-signatures.title: Contracts and signatures ⋅ Billow
/help/contracts-and-signatures.description: How to add and sign a contract on an offer, the rules for signature images, how your client signs, where the signed PDF is kept, and how to invalidate a contract.
h2: Where the signed contract is kept
Turning the contract on or off
p: How to add and sign a contract on an offer, the rules for signature images, how your client signs, where the signed PDF is kept, and how to invalidate a contract.
A contract is an optional part of an offer. It carries two signatures, yours and your client’s. You sign first, before you send the offer, and your client signs when they accept it.
Open the project and click Edit Project.
Check the contract text on the left and edit it if needed.
On the right, check Full name and Company. They are filled in with your name and your workspace’s legal name.
Draw or upload your signature under Draw your signature.
Tick the consent line, which confirms that your electronic signature is legally binding.
Billow shows “Contract signed successfully.” The Contract step then shows your name and company with “Signed on” and the date.
The offer can’t be sent until you have signed. Signing is only possible while the project is Draft.

Billow generates the contract from your contract template, filled in with your project information and deliverables. The dialog, titled Revise & Sign Contract with the account’s name, lets you edit the wording for this offer only.
Load template… above the editor replaces the text with one of your templates: Fixed-fee or Retainer. If you have already edited the text, Billow asks first:
Replace contract? Loading a template will replace your current edits. This cannot be undone.
To keep your edits without signing, click Save as draft.

If the contract uses a value that Billow doesn’t have yet, such as an address, clicking Sign Contract opens the Complete contract details dialog. Fill in the missing values and click Save & Continue. Billow saves them for next time and signs the contract.

Some values belong to your workspace and only owners and admins can set them. If none of the missing values are ones you can fill in, the dialog reads “Only workspace admins can set the values below. Ask one to complete them, then sign again.”
You can draw your signature on the pad with a mouse, a trackpad or a finger. The bin icon above the pad clears it.
You can also upload an image instead. Drop the file onto the pad, or click the upload icon above it. The upload replaces anything drawn on the pad. The file has to be:
A file that breaks a rule is rejected with a message:
That file is not a PNG. Export your signature as a PNG with a transparent background from your signature tool.
That file is larger than 1 MB. Export your signature at a smaller size and try again.
That image has a solid background. Export your signature as a PNG with a transparent background from your signature tool.
Photos and flatbed scans fail the transparency rule. A solid background would show as a block around your signature on the contract.
Your client signs on the offer page when they accept the offer.

They enter their verification code, read the contract in full, and then sign it with their full name, their company, a drawn or uploaded signature, and the consent line. The same image rules apply to their upload.

Billow creates the signed contract at that moment. Your name, company and signature sit on one side and theirs on the other, each with the date it was signed. Any add-on your client declined is left out, and the fee in the contract is recalculated to match.
Billow stores the signed PDF with the project and emails it, attached alongside the accepted offer, to the person who accepted.

Your copy is the Contract button on the project overview. Once your client has signed, it downloads the stored file, so the contract stays exactly as they signed it even if your template, logo or details change later.
Your client’s copy is that email. The offer page stops offering documents once they sign, and tells them the documents were emailed.
Invalidating unsigns the contract so you can change it. You can invalidate while the project is Draft, Offer Pending or Rejected.
Confirm with Invalidate in the Invalidate contract? dialog.
Billow shows “Contract unsigned successfully.” Your edits to the contract text are kept. Sign again before you send.
Going back to the Essentials or Deliverables step of an offer with a signed contract opens the same dialog.
Clears both signatures and their images
Makes the link your client has stop working
Moves the project back to Draft if it was Offer Pending or Rejected
When you send the offer again, your client gets a new link and a new code. On a rejected offer, invalidating is how you change the terms and send it again.
On a draft without a signed contract, the Include a contract toggle changes straight away. If the offer is Offer Pending or Rejected, or the contract is signed, Billow asks you to confirm first.
Confirming unsigns a signed contract. On an Offer Pending or Rejected offer, it also moves the project back to Draft, and the link your client has stops working.
Your contract text is kept when you turn the contract off, and comes back if you turn it on again.
Once your client accepts, the contract is locked. The Include a contract toggle is disabled with “Can’t be changed once the project is active”.
The statuses a project moves through, what causes each change, how to cancel or delete a project, what you can still edit, and how projects count toward your plan.

/help/contract-templates.title: Setting up your contract templates ⋅ Billow
/help/contract-templates.description: How to edit your fixed-fee and retainer contract templates, insert variables, set your standard contract values, and when a project picks up your changes.
h2: Reset a template to the default
p: How to edit your fixed-fee and retainer contract templates, insert variables, set your standard contract values, and when a project picks up your changes.
Settings → Contracts holds the templates and standard values Billow drafts each project’s contract from. Everyone in the workspace can view the page, but only admins and owners can edit it.
The Default Templates card has two tabs, Fixed-fee and Retainer, with one template each. The payment terms of the two kinds of work differ, so each has its own wording.

Every new project’s contract starts from the Fixed-fee template. To use the Retainer template on a project, choose Load template… → Retainer in the project’s contract editor. See Contracts and signatures.
In the Default Templates card, open the Fixed-fee or Retainer tab.
Edit the text in the editor.
A variable is a placeholder that Billow replaces with the project’s data, such as the account’s name, the project name or your payment terms.
Type { where the variable should go.
Choose a variable from the list, or keep typing to filter it.
The list groups variables under Project, for data that comes from the project and its offer, and Settings, for the standard values further down this page.
Secondary Tax Rate only has a value when the project’s offer has a second tax rate.
Open the tab of the template you want to reset.
Click Reset to default, next to the tabs.
Reset template? Resetting will replace your current edits with the default template. This cannot be undone.
Only the template on the open tab is reset. Resetting the Fixed-fee template leaves the Retainer template untouched.
Resetting fills the editor without saving. Click Save templates to keep the result. If you leave the page instead, the reset is discarded.
The cards below the templates hold the values your templates refer to. Each card has its own Save button. None of the fields are required, so fill in the ones your templates use.
Communication tool, response time in hours, phone number, notification threshold in hours
Hourly rate, monthly hours, payment terms in days
City and country whose law applies

A project takes its own copy of the template text when its offer is created. From then on, editing the template in Settings → Contracts does not change that project’s contract. To change the wording of an existing project’s contract, edit it on the project itself.

Your standard values keep updating on a project’s contract until you sign it. After that, the contract stays as signed, except that its deliverables and totals still follow the upsells your client keeps or adds when they accept.
How to set your default currency, tax rate, deposit percentage and business targets, and what each default changes.

/help/client-view-offer.title: What your client sees when you send an offer ⋅ Billow
/help/client-view-offer.description: What your client receives when you send an offer, how they accept or reject it with their verification code, and what the offer page shows afterwards.
h1: What your client sees when you send an offer
h2: How your client accepts an offer with a contract
How your client accepts an offer without a contract
How your client rejects an offer
p: What your client sees when you send an offer
What your client receives when you send an offer, how they accept or reject it with their verification code, and what the offer page shows afterwards.

When you send an offer, your client receives an email with a link to the offer page and an 8-digit verification code. The email comes from your workspace’s legal name. Your client doesn’t need a Billow account to open the offer.
Your logo and your legal name sit at the top of the page. Below them, your client sees:
The offer title and “Offer for” their company
Recipient and Contractor, with their details and yours. Your tax registration numbers appear in the Contractor details.
The offer date and the Valid until date
Your offer note, under Summary, if you wrote one

Your deliverables under Scope, with descriptions, prices, and timelines where you set them. A deliverable priced by quantity also shows how its price adds up when the quantity isn’t 1, for example “3 × $400.00”.
The totals, with tax unless you have hidden it
A Payment Structure box if you set a deposit, for example “50% Upfront Deposit. You’ll receive an invoice after the project is accepted.”
A Contract box with a Download link, if the offer includes a contract
If you hid the deliverable prices, Scope lists each deliverable and add-on without its price, and only the totals show amounts. The PDF leaves out the Qty, Rate and Amount columns.

Your client can download the offer with Download PDF until they accept it or it is rejected, cancelled or completed. An expired offer can still be downloaded. On larger screens, the copy link button at the top of the page copies the link so they can forward it inside their company.
Your client sees the deliverables you marked as upsells as add-ons. Each one shows a green Add-On badge with a Decline action.
If your client clicks Decline, the badge turns red, the price is struck through, and it drops out of the total straight away. Add back on the red badge reverses it while they are still deciding.

If you set upsells to start unselected, each add-on starts with a blue Add-On badge and an Add action, and the total leaves it out. Once your client adds it, the badge turns green with a Remove action. Add-ons your client hasn’t added when they accept are treated like declined ones.
A declined add-on never reaches an invoice, and it is left out of the contract they sign.

The contract your client downloads from the Contract box follows their current choice. It lists the add-ons they have kept or added, and any amount in it includes them. While at least one add-on is selected, the box reads “Includes the add-ons you’ve selected.” below the Download link. The offer PDF lists every add-on, marked “(Add-on)”, or “(Optional add-on)” while add-ons start unselected.
Your client clicks Accept Offer at the top of the page, or View & sign contract below the totals.
They enter the 8-digit code from the email and click Continue.
The contract opens in full, headed “Your Contract with [your legal name]”. They click Sign Contract.
They fill in Full name and Company, and draw or upload their signature the same way you signed yours.
They tick the consent line, which confirms that their electronic signature is legally binding.
Checking the code at step 2 doesn’t use it up, so your client can close the dialog and come back later.
Your client clicks Accept Offer at the top of the page, or Accept this offer below the totals.
They enter the 8-digit code and click Continue.
In the Sign & Accept Offer dialog, they fill in Full name and Company and tick the consent line.
There is nothing to draw or upload.
Your client sees “Offer accepted successfully!”, and the page changes:

A banner reads “Project offer is now signed from both sides” and says that a copy of the signed documents was emailed to the signer. If you set a deposit, it also says the deposit invoice will arrive soon.
The actions are replaced by Project Offer Accepted, “Thank you for your business.”
Download PDF and the contract download are no longer available.
On your side, the project moves to Active, your invoices are drafted, and Billow emails the person who created the project.

Right after your client accepts, Billow emails the person who accepted, at the address their code was sent to. The email carries the accepted offer as a PDF, and the signed contract as a second PDF if the offer had one.
The email comes from your legal name. Replies go to the person who created the project, or to the workspace owner if that person has left the workspace.
This email is your client’s copy of the signed documents, because the offer page stops offering downloads once they sign. Your copies are on the project page.
Your client clicks Reject below the totals.
They enter the 8-digit code and click Reject Offer.
Billow asks for no reason or comment. Your client sees “Offer rejected”, and Billow emails the person who created the project. The page then shows:
Offer Rejected You rejected this offer. Contact [your legal name] if you’d like to revisit it.
Your client can open the offer without the code. They need it to accept or reject.
Each code works once. After it has been used to accept or reject, the offer is decided and can’t be acted on again.
The code doesn’t expire on its own. It works while the offer is Offer Pending and before its Valid until date has passed.
Nobody can look up a code once it’s sent. If your client loses it, resend the offer.
Resending the offer to the same email address replaces your client’s code and leaves the offer and its link unchanged.
The code doesn’t match this offer, or it was replaced by a newer code sent to the same address
This offer has expired and cannot be accepted or rejected.
The Valid until date has passed
This offer is no longer open and cannot be accepted or rejected.
The offer was already accepted, rejected, cancelled or completed

If the offer expires, or is accepted, rejected, cancelled or completed, while your client is in the middle of accepting or rejecting it, the steps close, the message appears, and the page shows the offer as it stands now.

Withdrawing the offer to Draft is different: the link stops working, so your client can no longer open the offer. If your client is in the middle of accepting or rejecting it at that moment, their next step shows a Page Not Found error instead of a message. See Projects and their statuses.
Once the Valid until date has passed, the Accept and Reject actions disappear and the page shows:
Offer Expired This offer is no longer valid. Contact [your legal name] for an updated one.
The link keeps working after the offer is decided. What it shows depends on how the offer ended.
The offer in full while the project runs, with the scope, the totals and the date they accepted. Declined add-ons are no longer listed.
The title, who it was for, the offer date, the date they rejected it, and the Offer Rejected panel
The title, who it was for, the offer date, the date they accepted if they had, and the panel Offer Cancelled: “[your legal name] withdrew this offer. Contact them if you have questions.”
The title, who it was for, the offer date, the date they accepted, and the panel Project Completed: “All deliverables in this offer have been delivered. Thank you for working with us.”
On a rejected, cancelled or completed offer, your client no longer sees the deliverables, prices, taxes, deposit, offer note, contract or either address. Only the names and dates listed above remain.
The statuses a project moves through, what causes each change, how to cancel or delete a project, what you can still edit, and how projects count toward your plan.

/help/client-view-invoice.title: What your client sees when you send an invoice ⋅ Billow
/help/client-view-invoice.description: What is on the invoice page your client opens, how they pay by card or bank transfer, and how long the link keeps working.
h1: What your client sees when you send an invoice
p: What your client sees when you send an invoice
What is on the invoice page your client opens, how they pay by card or bank transfer, and how long the link keeps working.
Your client opens the invoice from a link, either in the email you send or one you share yourself. They do not need an account, a login or a verification code.
From top to bottom, the page shows:
Your logo and legal name, with a Download PDF button, and a Pay now button if the invoice is paid by card and still unpaid
The invoice title, or “Invoice” if it has none, the issue date, and the amount in large type
The due date, or “Due upon receipt”
To and From blocks with both addresses, your client’s VAT ID if it is on their account, and your tax registration numbers under yours
The line items and totals, with a status badge. If you hid the deliverable prices, the line items show no prices and only the totals carry amounts.
Your note, if you added one
The Payment section, until the invoice is paid or refunded
The invoice is sent and not yet paid
The due date has passed and the invoice is not paid. An invoice due upon receipt stays Unpaid

A deposit invoice shows a badge with its percentage, such as “50% Deposit”, next to the total project amount. It lists the full project scope and bills only the deposit amount. See Deposits and automatic invoices.
If the invoice’s payment method is Card Payment (Stripe), your client pays like this:
They click Pay now at the top, or the Pay [amount] with Card button in the Payment section.
Stripe’s checkout page opens, and they enter their card details there.
After paying, they return to a confirmation page from Billow.
The confirmation page reads Payment Successful. If Stripe has not confirmed the payment yet, it reads Payment Processing instead. A View Invoice button leads back to the invoice.
The invoice changes to Paid once Stripe confirms the payment, without any action from you.
The card buttons only appear while your workspace has an active Stripe connection. See Accepting card payments with Stripe.
If the invoice’s payment method is Bank Transfer, the Payment section asks your client to transfer the total using the invoice number as the reference. The invoice number has its own copy button.
Your bank details follow, each with a copy button:
Account Holder, Account Number, Routing Number
Bank Address also appears when the account has one.
Billow is not notified when a bank transfer arrives. You mark the invoice as paid yourself. See Getting paid.
You can copy the invoice link and send it to your client yourself. Copying the link of a draft sends it: the invoice moves to Pending and you can no longer edit it. See Share the link instead.
The link keeps working after the invoice is paid or refunded, so your client can come back to download the PDF. If you delete the invoice, its link stops working until you restore it.
Billow does not send your client a payment confirmation. For card payments, Stripe may send its own receipt. For bank transfers, your client receives nothing.
What Billow drafts when your client accepts an offer, how the deposit percentage sets the schedule, how to send the drafts, and how to create a deposit invoice yourself.

/help/building-and-sending-an-offer.title: Building and sending an offer ⋅ Billow
/help/building-and-sending-an-offer.description: How to build an offer in the project wizard, how to send it to your client or copy its link, and what sending changes.
h2: Add a timeline to a deliverable
Mark a deliverable as an upsell
Let your client opt in to upsells
Hide deliverable prices from your client
Adding an offer to a simple project
p: How to build an offer in the project wizard, how to send it to your client or copy its link, and what sending changes.

An offer lists what you will deliver for a client and what it costs. You build it in a four-step wizard (Essentials, Deliverables, Contract and Review) and then send it from the project page. Any member of the workspace can build and send offers.
Go to Projects and click New Project.
Fill in the Essentials step, then click Next: Deliverables.
Add your deliverables and check the financials, then click Next: Contract.
Turn on Include a contract and sign it if you want one, then click Review Offer.
Check the Review step and click Finish.
Finish marks the offer as reviewed and takes you back to the project page. Nothing is sent to your client yet.
To stop partway through, click Save as Draft and continue later from the project page with Continue Setup. The Review step doesn’t have Save as Draft.

While a step is incomplete, its next button and Save as Draft are disabled. On the Contract step, a contract that is turned on but not signed counts as incomplete. Once the project has been saved, the next button’s tooltip lists what is missing, for example “Missing: Account”.
The client company. You can create a new account from the dropdown.
The contact who receives the offer. You can create a new contact from the dropdown.
The date on the offer. It defaults to today.
The date the offer expires. It defaults to 30 days from today.
A description for your team. It is internal only and never shown to your client.
Each deliverable is one line on the offer, with a title, an optional description and a price. Click the + button below the list to add one.
Every line has one of two pricing modes:
How the line total is calculated
One price for the whole line
A rate multiplied by a quantity
Every deliverable needs a title. The offer needs at least one deliverable before you can continue.
The Offer note field sits above the deliverables. Your client sees it on the offer page and on the PDF, so use it to describe the scope of the project.
The Financials section below the deliverables sets how the offer is billed. Its values start from your defaults in Settings → Accounting, and any change applies to this project only.
The share of the total your client pays upfront: None, 25%, 33%, 50% or 100%. It also appears in your contract’s payment terms.
The tax rate. If you leave it empty or set 0%, the tax line is hidden on the final document.
With advanced tax mode on, the tax field is replaced by Tax Label, Tax Rate (%), Second Tax Label and Second Tax Rate (%).
Set the deposit before you send. It decides which invoices Billow drafts once your client accepts. Deposits and automatic invoices lists what each option produces.
Timelines are optional date ranges on a deliverable.
Click Add Timeline next to the deliverable’s title.
Pick the start and end dates.
The range then shows as a badge on the line. Click the × on the badge to remove it.
A timeline appears under its deliverable on the Review step, on the project page, on your client’s offer page, and on the PDF. Invoices don’t show it.
An upsell is a deliverable your client can decline when they accept the offer. Billow calls it an upsell in the app, and your client sees it as an add-on on the offer page and in the PDF.
Find the deliverable in the list.

On the offer page, the line carries a green Add-On badge with a Decline action. If your client declines it, the line drops out of the offer total and never reaches an invoice or the contract they sign.
The first deliverable can’t be an upsell.

Upsells start selected on the offer page, so the total your client sees first includes them. If you turn on Upsells start unselected, they start unselected instead. The total then shows only the base scope, and each upsell your client adds is added on top.
On the Deliverables step, click the settings button next to the Deliverables heading.

The setting is saved with the rest of the Deliverables step. The Deliverables step, the Review step and the project page show the base total with a With all upsells line below it. The offer PDF lists upsells as optional add-ons and leaves them out of the total.
To start every new offer this way, an owner or admin ticks Upsells start unselected in new offers in Settings → Accounting. Changing it doesn’t affect offers that already exist.

Your client sees the price of each deliverable on the offer page and in the PDF. If you turn on Hide deliverable prices, they see the deliverables and upsells without their prices, and only the subtotal, taxes and total carry amounts.
To keep the price of each upsell visible, turn on Show upsell prices below it.

The setting is saved with the rest of the Deliverables step and changes no amounts. Your client can still decline or add upsells, and the total follows their choice. The offer PDF leaves out its Qty, Rate and Amount columns.

With Show upsell prices on, your client sees the price of each upsell while the other deliverables stay without prices. The offer PDF keeps its Qty, Rate and Amount columns and fills them in for the upsells only. Show upsell prices appears only while Hide deliverable prices is on.

The Deliverables step, the Review step and the project page keep showing every price, with “Deliverable prices are hidden from the client. They see the totals only.” below the totals. With Show upsell prices on, the note reads “Deliverable prices are hidden from the client, except for the upsells. They see each upsell’s price and the totals.” Invoices drafted when your client accepts the offer start with the same Hide deliverable prices setting and hide every line’s price, upsells included, since invoices have no upsells. To start every new offer this way, an owner or admin ticks Hide deliverable prices, and optionally Show upsell prices, in Settings → Accounting. Changing them doesn’t affect offers that already exist.

Contracts are optional. The Include a contract toggle on the Contract step is off on new offers. When you turn it on, Billow generates a contract from your template, and you must sign it before you can continue to the Review step. See Contracts and signatures.
If the offer has no contract, you don’t sign anything. Your client still signs the offer when they accept it.
The Review step shows everything the offer will say: the essentials, the deliverables and financials, and the contract. Preview Offer opens the page your client will see.
Click Finish to mark the offer as reviewed. Finishing requires at least one deliverable, and a signed contract if the offer includes one.
If you change the project or the offer after finishing, the reviewed mark is cleared while the offer is still a draft. Go through the Review step and click Finish again before you send.
Click Send Offer at the top of the page. Once the offer is ready, the same button also appears in the banner “Your offer is complete. Send it to your client to get it signed.”
If a detail is missing, fill it in and click Save & Continue.
Check the email address under Sending to.
Billow shows “Offer sent successfully.” and the project moves to Offer Pending.
Billow checks the recipient and both addresses before the confirmation opens. Anything missing is collected first, in one dialog titled Add details to send.
The dialog “No contact selected” opens. Click Choose a contact to pick one on the Essentials step, then send again.
The dialog asks for it and saves it to the contact.
The dialog asks for it and saves it to the account.
Owners and admins can fill it in, and it is saved to your workspace. Members see that an admin has to add it.
If you are a member and your company’s address is the only thing missing, the dialog reads:
Workspace address required A workspace admin needs to add your company’s address before this offer can be sent.
Your company’s address lives on Settings → General.
While the offer isn’t ready, Send Offer is disabled and its tooltip says why.
Add at least one deliverable before sending.
Add a deliverable on the Deliverables step.
Sign the contract on the Contract step, or turn the contract off.
Update the valid until date before sending.
Move Offer Valid Until to today or later on the Essentials step.
Go through the Review step and click Finish.
An offer is valid until the end of its Offer Valid Until date.
Billow assigns the offer number, for example OFF-2026-0001. Numbers count up per year, and drafts don’t have one.
The project moves to Offer Pending.
Your client receives an email with the link and an 8-digit verification code. The email comes from your workspace’s legal name.
Preview Offer on the project overview opens the client-facing page as your client will see it, with its buttons disabled.
After you send the offer, the button reads View Offer. It disappears when the project is Rejected, Cancelled or Completed.
Once the offer is sent, you can share its link through your own channels as well as the email Billow sends.
Click Copy Public Link on the project overview, next to View Offer.
Billow copies the link to your clipboard and confirms with “Link copied to clipboard”.
Copying the link doesn’t send anything or change the project. Copy Public Link disappears when the project is Rejected, Cancelled or Completed.
Anyone with the link can open the offer. Accepting or rejecting it still takes the verification code from the email. See What your client sees.
Your client accepts or rejects the offer from the link. Billow emails the person who created the project either way. What your client sees walks through both.
To give your client a new code, resend the offer. Resending leaves the offer and its link unchanged.
If the Offer Valid Until date passes without a decision, Billow emails the person who created the offer. Nothing is sent to your client automatically.
Click Edit Project on the project page to change an offer that is Offer Pending or Rejected. Going back to the Essentials or Deliverables step asks for confirmation first:
Revokes the sent offer, moves the project to Draft, and invalidates the share link
Moves the project to Draft and invalidates the share link
If the offer has a signed contract, the dialog is Invalidate contract? instead, and confirming also unsigns the contract. See Contracts and signatures.
When you send the offer again, your client gets a new link and a new code.
You can turn a simple project into an offer with Turn into offer. Saving the Essentials step then asks for confirmation:

Turn this project into an offer? Saving this step creates an offer and moves the project from Active to Draft. It becomes Active again once your client accepts the offer. The offer cannot be removed later.

/help/bank-accounts.title: Adding a bank account ⋅ Billow
/help/bank-accounts.description: How to add, edit and delete the bank accounts printed on bank transfer invoices, and how the primary account works.
p: How to add, edit and delete the bank accounts printed on bank transfer invoices, and how the primary account works.

Bank accounts hold the payment details Billow prints on invoices paid by bank transfer, so your client knows where to pay. You manage them in the Bank Accounts card on Settings → Accounting. Only owners and admins can add, edit or delete an account.
In the Bank Accounts card, click Add Bank Account.
Choose an Account Type: IBAN, US (ACH) or Other.
Fill in Account Name, Currency and the fields for that type.
The account appears in the Bank Accounts card with its currency and details. There is no limit on how many accounts you add, and they can be in different currencies.
Once you have at least one account, you can add another while you write an invoice: click Add new next to the Bank Account field.
The fields change with the type. Account Type starts on US (ACH) if your workspace’s country is the United States, and on IBAN otherwise.
Account Number and Routing Number, both required. The routing number must be exactly 9 digits.
Use Other for anything that doesn’t fit the first two. Billow prints whatever you type on the invoice as-is.
A label for you, such as “Business Checking”
The name on the account. If you leave it blank, Billow uses your workspace’s legal name.
Click the pencil icon on the account.
Drafts pick up the new details. Invoices you already sent keep the details they were sent with.
One account is the primary, marked with a Primary badge. The first account you add becomes the primary automatically.
The Bank Account field on a new invoice starts on the primary account. An invoice without an account of its own also uses the primary.
Click the pencil icon on the account you want as primary.
Tick Set as primary bank account.
The Primary badge moves to that account. You can also tick Set as primary bank account when you add a new account.

An invoice and its bank account don’t need the same currency. A EUR invoice can point at a USD account. When they differ, the invoice form shows a warning, for example “This account is in USD, but the invoice is in EUR. Your bank may apply conversion fees.” Nothing blocks you from saving.

An invoice carries one payment method: Bank Transfer or Card Payment (Stripe). If you have at least one bank account, new invoices start on Bank Transfer, even when Stripe is connected. Choose Card Payment (Stripe) on each invoice where you want it.
If you choose Bank Transfer before adding any account, the invoice form shows “You first need to add a bank account to use Bank Transfer” with a Set up now button.
Billow copies your bank details onto an invoice at the moment you send it. Editing or deleting the account later doesn’t change a document your client already has.
Click the trash icon on the account.
Click Delete Bank Account in the dialog.
Delete Bank Account Are you sure you want to delete [account name]? Invoices you have already sent keep the bank details they were sent with. This action cannot be undone.
If you delete the primary account, the oldest remaining account becomes the primary.

You can’t delete a bank account while an unpaid bank transfer invoice uses it. Choose a different Bank Account on those invoices first. If it’s your primary account, make another account primary first, because invoices without an account of their own use the primary.
Billow tells you why after you confirm, for example:
Cannot delete: unpaid bank transfer invoices still use this account for payment details. Re-point those invoices to another account first.

/help/adding-accounts-and-contacts.title: Adding accounts and contacts ⋅ Billow
/help/adding-accounts-and-contacts.description: How to add an account and its contacts, the fields on each, the figures on the accounts list, and what blocks a delete.
h3: Account statuses: Healthy, Risky, Inactive and Churned
p: How to add an account and its contacts, the fields on each, the figures on the accounts list, and what blocks a delete.
An account is a company you do work for. A contact is a person at that company.
Projects belong to an account, and every offer and invoice is tied to one. Leads need both an account and a contact before you can save them.
Fill in any of the optional fields.
The account appears on the accounts list. You can change any field later from Edit in the account’s … menu.
The company’s name. It has to be unique in your workspace.
Free text, used by the Industry filter on the accounts list
A JPG or PNG image of at least 200×200 px and up to 5 MB
If the name is already taken, you see “An account with this name already exists in your workspace.”

To add the person of contact while you create the account, type their name in Person of Contact and choose Create new contact. Fill in the Add Contact panel that opens and click Add Contact. Billow saves the contact together with the account when you click Create Account.
Choose the Associated Account, or type a new company name and create the account from there.
A contact belongs to exactly one account, and an account can have as many contacts as you need.
The company the person works at
Is Primary Contact of this Account
Makes this person the account’s primary contact
A link to their LinkedIn profile

Each account has at most one primary contact. If the account already has one and you save a contact with Is Primary Contact of this Account ticked, Billow asks you to confirm in the Change Primary Contact dialog. The new contact replaces the old one as primary.
A contact is used in two places: as the main contact on a project, and as the billing contact on an invoice.
Two tabs sit above the list.
Contacts you haven’t archived, at accounts you haven’t marked as churned
Contacts you archived, and every contact of an account you marked as churned
The list can be filtered by account, status, role, type and the date the contact was added, and sorted by Name, Account, Role or Added on. See Filtering and sorting lists.
Open the contact, or find it on the contacts list.
If the contact is the account’s primary contact, the Archive Primary Contact dialog asks you to confirm. Archiving removes their primary status.
To bring a contact back, choose Unarchive from the same menu. A contact of a churned account returns to All when the account is restored.
Each row shows the money that account has made you.
Total revenue from this account, all time
Their share of your total earnings, with churned accounts excluded

Healthy and Risky accounts come first, with overdue invoices ahead within that group, then Inactive. Clicking a column header sorts by that column instead. The Filter menu narrows the list by status, industry, LTV or the date the account was added. See Filtering and sorting lists.
Only owners and admins can delete accounts and contacts. Delete sits in the … menu on the list and at the bottom of the account or contact page.
Billow blocks the delete while the record is still in use:
It has any project or lead, or any invoice
A project, lead or invoice uses it

If the delete is blocked, or you aren’t an owner or admin, Delete doesn’t appear in the … menu on the list. The Delete button at the bottom of the account or contact page is greyed out, and hovering over it shows the reason. For a contact in use, it reads “Cannot delete a contact that is referenced by projects or invoices.”
Billow has no trash for accounts and contacts. Deleting one removes it from your workspace with no undo in the app. To keep the records of an account that has gone quiet, mark it as churned instead.

/help/accounting-setup.title: Setting up your accounting defaults ⋅ Billow
/help/accounting-setup.description: How to set your default currency, tax rate, deposit percentage and business targets, and what each default changes.
p: How to set your default currency, tax rate, deposit percentage and business targets, and what each default changes.
Settings → Accounting holds the defaults every new offer and invoice starts from. Everyone in the workspace can see the page, but only owners and admins can change it.
Change the fields you need in the Financial Defaults card.
Click Save at the bottom of the card.
Billow confirms with “Finance settings updated successfully.”
The new defaults apply to offers, invoices and projects you create from now on. Billow never rewrites an offer or invoice you already created.
Preselected on new invoices, offers and projects. It is also the currency your Cockpit converts its totals into.
Pre-fills the tax rate on new invoices and offers. Leave it empty if you don’t charge tax.
Adds an editable tax label and an optional second tax line. See Taxes on your documents.
Offers show only the subtotal, with no tax line. Invoices always include tax.

New offers, and new invoices without an offer, hide each deliverable’s price from your client, who sees only the totals. An invoice for a project with an offer follows that offer instead. You can change it per offer or invoice.
Appears below Hide deliverable prices while it is ticked. New offers keep each upsell’s price visible to your client while the other deliverables stay without prices. You can change it per offer.
Upsells start unselected in new offers
New offers start with their upsells unselected, so your client opts in to each one. You can change it per offer.
Sets how much of a project you bill up front, and drives Billow’s automatic invoice drafting. The options are None, 25%, 33%, 50% and 100%. New workspaces start at 50%.
Deposits and automatic invoices covers what each deposit percentage produces.
If Billow knows the usual VAT rate for your workspace’s country, a hint appears under Default VAT Percentage (%): “Workspaces in [country] typically use [rate]%.” Click the rate to fill it in.

Advanced tax mode adds an editable tax label and an optional second tax line, for places like Quebec that charge two taxes on the same document. You can override both on any individual invoice or offer.
Taxes on your documents covers the full setup.
Both fields are optional. They only feed your Cockpit, and nothing else in Billow depends on them.
What it powers on your Cockpit
The Yearly Revenue Target card, which shows your progress toward the target
The Costs Covered This Month card and the break-even line on the revenue chart
Until you fill them in, those Cockpit cards show a prompt that links to Settings → Accounting.
The Bank Accounts and Card Payments cards further down the same page decide how your clients can pay you. See Adding a bank account and Accepting card payments with Stripe.
Your legal name, address, country and tax registration numbers live on Settings → General.
Your legal name is also the sender name on every email a client receives from Billow, offer and invoice notifications included.

/help/account-health.title: Account statuses: Healthy, Risky, Inactive and Churned ⋅ Billow
/help/account-health.description: The four account statuses and their thresholds, what counts as activity, and how to mark an account as churned or restore it.
h1: Account statuses: Healthy, Risky, Inactive and Churned
p: Account statuses: Healthy, Risky, Inactive and Churned
The four account statuses and their thresholds, what counts as activity, and how to mark an account as churned or restore it.
Billow gives each account a status based on how recently it had activity. Billow works the status out for you. The only manual control is marking an account as churned.
The account had activity recently and has nothing overdue
The account has overdue invoices, has had no activity for 60 days or more, or makes up more than 35% of your total earnings
The account has had no activity for 120 days or more, or has nothing on record yet
The account has had no activity for 12 months or more, or you marked it as churned
When more than one status fits, Churned comes first, then Inactive, then Risky.
Healthy and Risky accounts count as active. That same rule decides the Active Accounts figure on the accounts list and on your Cockpit.
On the accounts list, the Status column shows invoice alerts in place of Healthy, Risky or Inactive when there are any:
The account has invoices past their due date
The account has unpaid invoices that are not due yet
Work on a project or a live lead
Leads you marked Unqualified or Lost never count.
Leads on their own are not enough either. Until an account has at least one real project or one invoice, it stays Inactive.
Two tabs sit above the accounts list.
Every account that is not churned
A churned account appears on the Churned tab only. To narrow the All tab to one status, use the Status filter. Filtering and sorting lists lists every option.
Open the account, or find it on the accounts list.
Billow confirms with “Account ‘[name]’ marked as churned.”
The account moves to the Churned tab straight away, whatever its activity says.
The account no longer has an RS figure on the accounts list, and your other accounts’ RS is worked out without its earnings. Any account whose RS goes above 35% becomes Risky.
Its contacts move to the Archived tab of the contacts list.
Nothing is deleted. Projects, invoices and history stay where they are.
Open the churned account, or find it on the Churned tab.
Billow confirms with “Account ‘[name]’ restored.” Restoring counts as activity, so the account usually comes back as Healthy.
A restored account with no further activity churns again 12 months later.
